fullText:
Summary: JAT Holdings (JAT.N0000) is growing fast after expanding into New Zealand and Bangladesh, but the price is well ahead of what its returns support. At Rs 37.10 it trades at 1.58x its NAV of Rs 23.48 and 12.0x trailing earnings, with a 1.9% dividend yield. Return on equity has been 11–17% (13% in the year to March 2026), below the 18% return I require, so the book-value methods value it below NAV, and only the P/E method supports today's price. Averaging the methods gives a fair value of about Rs 21, so the price is about 77% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 17.80 and treat under Rs 15.70 as a strong buy. Sales rose 36% in the first half, but costs rose almost as fast and the business used cash to build inventory.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 37.10 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-06). Please check it live. In July–September 2026 it traded between Rs 32.40 and Rs 40.20, after Rs 35.00–44.00 in April–June, and it closed the year to March 2026 at Rs 39.00.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue rose 36% to Rs 7.01bn and profit attributable to shareholders rose 24% to Rs 497mn. EPS was Rs 0.95 against Rs 0.77.
What drove it: the new New Zealand business (Mirotone) added Rs 693mn of sales, Bangladesh grew 49% to Rs 1.56bn, and Sri Lanka grew 14% to Rs 4.56bn. Wood coatings rose 34% and decoratives 83%; EV chargers fell 5%. But selling costs rose 48% and administration 32%, so operating profit rose only 15%. Finance costs fell 30%.
Cash: operating cash flow was negative (Rs 46mn outflow) because inventory rose Rs 1.13bn and advances Rs 0.65bn. Borrowings (including overdrafts) were Rs 4.38bn against cash and short-term investments of Rs 1.46bn.
Year to March 2026 (group): revenue Rs 12.64bn (up 9%), profit Rs 1.52bn (down 14%, after a tax credit the year before), EPS Rs 2.92 (Rs 3.50), ROE 13%, NAV Rs 23.13. Inventory took 154 days to sell and customers 139 days to pay.
Dividend: Rs 376mn was paid in the half (about Rs 0.72 a share); the annual report lists Rs 0.44 a share for 2025/26.

Methods
NAV (Rs 23.48): 1.58x, so it fails your NAV rule.
Return on equity: 13% (year to March 2026). Earlier years: 17% (2025), 11% (2024), 15% (2023), 16% (2022).
P/E: 12.0x trailing EPS of Rs 3.10. Year-end P/E: 13.4x (2026), 7.7x (2025).
Dividends: about Rs 0.72 paid this year, a 1.9% yield; the company pays out 15–25% of profit.
Debt: gearing 21% and net debt Rs 2.19bn at March 2026; borrowings rose in the half to fund inventory.
Justified price to book: Rs 11.0 / 15.7 / 24.7 across the cases, weighted Rs 16.1.
P/E method: Rs 23.2 / 34.0 / 45.6, weighted Rs 33.1.
Residual income: Rs 7.1 / 13.3 / 24.4, weighted Rs 13.7.
Dividend model: Rs 2.9 / 6.4 / 10.4 (not used in the fair value).

JAT keeps most of its profit, so a dividend model understates it, and with heavy working capital its free cash flow is too irregular for a reliable DCF, so I used three methods. The P/E method is far more generous than the book-value methods because the market pays about 10x earnings for growth, while ROE is below the 18% required return.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 20% / 18% / 16.5%.
Long-run ROE (price to book): 12% / 14% / 17%.
ROE path (residual income): 13% falling to 11% / 14.5% falling to 14% / 16% rising to 17%.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 2.9 × 8 / 3.4 × 10 / 3.8 × 12.
Average of the three methods: Rs 13.8 / Rs 21.0 / Rs 31.6.
Common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (October 2026), plus a premium for a small, export-exposed manufacturer. In the base case, the second half grows about 15% on last year's (helped by New Zealand), giving EPS of about Rs 3.40 for the year to March 2027.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 21.00 (0.89x NAV), so Rs 37.10 is about 77% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 17.80, and 25% gives Rs 15.70.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 21.00, 150 at up to Rs 17.80 and 150 at up to Rs 15.70. That averages about Rs 18.45, about Rs 9,225, against Rs 18,550 at Rs 37.10.
Realism: Rs 21 needs about a 43% fall and Rs 17.80 about 52%. The share was Rs 26.90 in March 2025, so it has been there recently, but it would take a market sell-off or a profit disappointment.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 16%: 11.3 / 17.4 / 24.7 for long-run ROE of 11% / 14% / 17%.
Cost of equity 18%: 8.9 / 13.3 / 18.5.
Cost of equity 20%: 7.2 / 10.5 / 14.3.
On book value, today's price would need ROE well above 17% for years.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: the New Zealand and Bangladesh businesses lifting ROE above 17%; costs growing slower than sales; inventory and receivables falling, turning cash flow positive; a higher dividend payout; lower interest rates.
Supports a lower value: costs continuing to rise as fast as sales; more cash tied up in inventory (154 days) and receivables (139 days); integration problems with the overseas acquisitions; a construction or furniture-export slowdown hitting wood coatings; currency swings in Bangladesh and New Zealand.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
